hook: GPT-6.2 Sol lists $2 input and $10 output per million tokens at standard short-context rates, but does not support Flex. The November 10 worked example compares Claude Sonnet 5.5 with GPT-6.1 Sol. Equal rates do not establish equal costs for the same documents.

sections.title: November 20 update: GPT-6.2 pricing and service tiers
sections.content:
Standard short-context rates, checked 20 November 2026 (USD per million tokens).

| Model | Input | Output | Cache read | 30m cache write | 12h cache write |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-6.2 Sol | $2.00 | $10.00 | $0.10 | $2.50 | $5.00 |
| GPT-6.2 Astra | $8.00 | $40.00 | $0.40 | $10.00 | $20.00 |

Through 272,000 input tokens use the short-context rate. Above that, input and cache rates double and output rises to 1.5x for the full request, not just the excess.

Short-context Batch input/output is $1/$5 for Sol and $4/$20 for Astra. Neither GPT-6.2 model supports Flex. Flex remains available for listed older models during the beta wind-down. There is no confirmed retirement date.

The worked examples below retain the November 10 model selection and November 13 corrections, not a new GPT-6.2 benchmark.

sections.title: The tokenizer note is not a cross-vendor benchmark
sections.content:
Anthropic describes roughly 30% more tokens for some inputs under its newer tokenizer, compared with earlier Claude models, not between Claude and GPT. Count the same input separately for each target model and record generated output separately.

The $1,844 bill assumes equal token counts. Its input-only sensitivity case keeps the $500 output line unchanged; neither case measures a cross-vendor token ratio.

Correction, 13 November 2026: removed the unsupported cross-vendor 30% claim and the whole-bill multiplier. Cache controls, hit rates and reuse arithmetic were also corrected on this date; other rates retain their original verification date.

sections.title: Caching is a break-even test, not a discount
sections.content:
In the November 10 standard short-context comparison, Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol both cost $2 input, $10 output and $0.10 per million cache reads (0.05x).

| Cache operation | Sonnet 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|
| Short write | 1.25x, 5m | 1.25x, 30m |
| Long write | 2x, 1h | 2.5x, 12h |
| Hit | 0.05x | 0.05x |

Let n be total requests, including the cold first request. One write and n-1 successful full-prefix reads cost w + r(n-1), not w + rn. This excludes fresh input and output and assumes no intervening expiry, prefix change or rewrite.

Short writes: 1.25 + 0.05(n-1) < n means n > 1.2632. At ten requests, 1.25 + 0.05 × 9 = 1.70 versus 10 uncached: 83% less for this prefix alone. With a 0.1x model the corresponding total is 2.15, a 78.5% reduction.

Long writes at 0.05x reads need three total requests (one write, two hits): Sonnet costs 2.10 and Sol costs 2.60 versus 3 uncached. Never count an expired entry as a hit.

sections.title: Batch is the one line where both sheets agree
sections.content:
Both vendors halve input and output in the listed Batch rows. The November 10 GPT-6.1 Sol Batch and Flex prices match; GPT-6.2 supports Batch, not Flex.

| Batch, per million | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Claude Opus 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | $1.00 | $2.00 | $1.00 |
| Output | $5.00 | $10.00 | $5.00 |

Anthropic's page says its cache multipliers stack with the batch discount. For Sonnet 5.5, apply the 0.05x hit multiplier to the applicable batch input rate only for an actual cache hit; a batch does not guarantee reuse. If there are no hits, a short-window cold cache write costs 25% more than the same uncached batch input.

sections.title: Long prompts are where the sheets stop being comparable
sections.content:
Both vendors reprice the prompt once it gets long, and they do it in different shapes.

| Prompt size | GPT-6.1 Sol | Claude Haiku 5.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Short context, input | $2.00 | $0.10 up to 100,000 tokens |
| Long context, input | $4.00 | $0.50 over 100,000 tokens |
| Long context, output | $15.00 | $2.50 over 100,000 tokens |

OpenAI's long-context row doubles input and multiplies output by 1.5. Anthropic's Haiku sheet lists two rows, one for prompts up to 100,000 tokens and one for prompts over it, at five times the rate, and it does not print a marginal split.

A 200,000-token prompt therefore bills at 0.2 × $0.50 = $0.10 on the over-100k row against $0.02 if the same prompt fit under the line. That cliff, not the per-token sticker, is what a document pipeline hits when someone pastes a whole contract set.

sections.title: Three add-ons that quietly change the unit
sections.content:
Fast mode on both sides doubles the sticker: Opus 5.5 goes to $8 input and $40 output, GPT-6.1 Sol to $4 and $20. Anthropic notes that fast mode is not available with the Batch API, so the two savings cannot be stacked.

Data residency is a multiplier rather than a tier. Sending Claude 4.6 or later to US-only inference applies 1.1x to every token category, cache writes and reads included.

For exactly two requests 12 hours apart, with no intervening reuse: Anthropic's 1-hour entry has expired: two cold writes cost 2 + 2 = 4 prefix units, not 2 + a cache read. 

For GPT-6.1 Sol, a successful 12-hour-cache hit would cost 2.5 + 0.05 = 2.55 across the pair; two cold writes cost 5. Both exceed two uncached passes at 2. 

This is not a long-run forecast: measure hits, writes and refreshes before extrapolating.

cost_math.label: 100k requests, 16k cached prefix, 4k fresh input, 500 output
cost_math.result: $1,844 with the stated equal billed token counts and rates; not a measured same-text comparison; assumes fresh input lies after the explicit cache breakpoint and is not written

cost_math.label: Hypothetical sensitivity: 30% more input-category tokens, output unchanged
cost_math.formula: Input categories: ($400 writes + $144 hits + $800 fresh input) × 1.30 = $1,747.20; unchanged output $500; total $2,247.20
cost_math.result: $403.20 above the $1,844 baseline (21.87%). Assumed input change only, not an observed Claude-versus-GPT difference.

cost_math.label: One write plus n-1 reads of one unchanged prefix
cost_math.formula: Sonnet 5.5 / GPT-6.1 Sol short write: 1.25 + 0.05(n-1) < n; n > 1.2632. At n=10: 1.25 + 9 × 0.05 = 1.70 versus 10. Long write at n=3: Sonnet 2 + 2 × 0.05 = 2.10; Sol 2.5 + 2 × 0.05 = 2.60 versus 3.
cost_math.result: Short window saves 83% on the cached prefix over ten requests. Long windows break even at three total requests, assuming two successful hits.

cost_math.label: Exactly two requests 12 hours apart, no intervening reuse
cost_math.formula: Sonnet 1h: two expired/cold writes, 2 + 2 = 4. Sol 12h if hit: 2.5 + 0.05 = 2.55; if miss and rewritten: 2.5 + 2.5 = 5. Uncached: 1 + 1 = 2.
cost_math.result: A 1-hour entry cannot be assumed to hit after 12 hours. Even the illustrative Sol hit costs more than two uncached passes; not a long-run schedule forecast.

decision_matrix.situation: A long, stable system prompt at high volume
decision_matrix.why: Compare measured input, cache-write, cache-hit and output usage at the applicable rates. The Claude tokenizer note does not supply a GPT comparison ratio.
The historical GPT-6.1 Sol rates double input and increase output by 1.5x above its own threshold. The separate Claude Haiku 5.5 boundary is 100,000 tokens.

decision_matrix.situation: Nightly batch of a few hundred thousand jobs
decision_matrix.why: The named Batch rows halve input and output rates; a short-window cold write without hits adds 25% to that portion of uncached batch input.

decision_matrix.situation: Only two requests, 12 hours apart, no intervening reuse
decision_matrix.why: Sonnet 1h writes cost 4 prefix units after expiry; Sol 12h costs 2.55 with one hit or 5 with a rewrite, versus 2 uncached. A recurring workload needs its own observed hit/write history.
Output is 5x input on both sheets, so the $10 against $20 output rate dominates the bill long before the input line does.

decision_matrix.situation: Streaming that a user is watching
decision_matrix.why: Opus 5.5 moves to $8 and $40 and GPT-6.1 Sol to $4 and $20, and fast mode cannot be combined with batch.

decision_matrix.situation: Data must stay in the US
decision_matrix.why: US-only inference multiplies every Claude token category by 1.1, cache writes and reads included, which changes a close comparison.

decision_matrix.situation: A prototype with prompts under 100,000 tokens
decision_matrix.why: $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million is a twentieth of the November 10 comparison rows, and the over-100k rate only applies when the prompt crosses the line.

verdict_summary: For the dated November 10 comparison, the named standard rows match: $2 input, $10 output and $0.10 cached input per million tokens. That does not make the same task equally expensive. Measure token usage, output quality, cache hits and retries on a representative sample. Apply the selected model, context and service-tier rates to those measurements; do not multiply a vendor bill by an assumed tokenizer premium.
migration_guide:
The historical worked example retains GPT-6.1 Sol; do not treat its service-tier support as a GPT-6.2 migration guide.

Caching controls are not interchangeable. Anthropic Messages is opt-in: top-level cache_control selects an automatic moving breakpoint; block-level cache_control selects explicit breakpoints. GPT-6.1 Sol supports implicit caching and explicit-only breakpoints. Re-measure token usage on migration, rather than transferring an assumed token ratio.

The worked bill uses explicit boundaries around the stable prefix, leaving fresh input outside the write. Batch jobs, files and model-specific configuration also need review when switching providers.

faqs.q: Is prompt caching automatic on both?
faqs.a: Anthropic Messages requires opt-in: use top-level cache_control for automatic breakpoint placement, or block-level cache_control for explicit boundaries. GPT-6.1 Sol supports implicit caching by default and explicit-only controls. Automatic placement does not guarantee a hit.

faqs.q: Do the batch discount and the cache discount combine?
faqs.a: Anthropic says cache multipliers stack with its batch discount. OpenAI publishes model-specific Batch and Flex tables: GPT-6.1 Sol appears in both, but GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra do not support Flex. A price match does not establish service-tier availability. Anthropic excludes fast mode from batch.

faqs.q: Does the 30% tokenizer note mean Claude costs 30% more than GPT?
faqs.a: No. Anthropic compares newer and earlier Claude tokenizers, not Claude with GPT. The difference depends on content. Measure each target model on the same input and account for generated output separately; this article provides no measured cross-vendor ratio.

faqs.q: Is a cache write ever a loss?
faqs.a: Yes. For Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, count one cold write plus n-1 hits across n requests, with a 0.05x hit rate. Short writes need two total requests; long writes need three. Expiry or changed prefixes add writes, not discounted reads.
